nary_nodes.label: 2026 Solar Eclipse
evidence: The UK and Europe have enjoyed their most dramatic solar eclipse for nearly 30 years, with millions thought to have witnessed the once-in-a-generation event.

nary_nodes.label: Partial Eclipse in UK
evidence: Those watching the astronomical phenomenon from the UK were treated to a partial eclipse, which peaked shortly after 19:00 BST, when most saw more than 90% of the Sun covered by the Moon.

nary_nodes.label: Total Eclipse in Greenland, Iceland, Spain
evidence: But parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain experienced the complete darkness and spectacle of a total eclipse.

nary_nodes.label: Universe is amazing
evidence: astronomy enthusiasts saying it served as a reminder of how "amazing" the Universe is.
"The Universe is amazing."

nary_nodes.label: Total Eclipse Path Start
evidence: The path of the total eclipse began at the northern tip of Siberia in Russia, far away from crowds and telescopes.

nary_nodes.label: Total Eclipse Path in Iceland
evidence: But it soon began curving around the Arctic Ocean arriving in Iceland in the early evening before sweeping southwards to treat the UK to part of its wonder.

nary_nodes.label: Partial Eclipse Start in Scotland
evidence: The partial eclipse began at about 18:00 BST in northern Scotland

nary_nodes.label: Partial Eclipse Start in England
evidence: and just before 18:20 on the south coast of England.

nary_nodes.label: Short Supply of Eclipse Glasses
evidence: Some had been successful in getting hold of solar eclipse glasses, but the vital eye protectors were in short supply in the run-up to the event with high-street shops and online suppliers all but sold out.

nary_nodes.label: Eclipse Glasses Sold in Unexpected Places
evidence: Stock turned up for sale in unexpected places as retailers sought to cash in on demand, including a central London bakery.

nary_nodes.label: Use of Improvised Viewers
evidence: colanders, cereal boxes and pieces of paper were deployed to offer them a glimpse of the partial eclipse safely.

nary_nodes.label: Definition of Solar Eclipse
evidence: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, blocking some or all of the Sun's light and casting a shadow on our planet.

nary_nodes.label: Sun, Moon, Earth not aligned from UK
evidence: As seen from the UK, the Sun, Moon and Earth were not quite directly in line.

nary_nodes.label: Sun, Moon, Earth perfectly aligned
evidence: At roughly 19:30 BST (20:30 local time), the Sun, Moon and Earth were perfectly aligned - a total eclipse.

nary_nodes.label: Yasmin Catricheo Travels for Eclipse
evidence: Chilean scientist Yasmin Catricheo, travelled thousands of miles to A Coruña, north-west Spain for the event.

nary_nodes.label: Totality was exciting and indescribable
evidence: "At the totality, everyone was cheering and sharing the excitement of what we were seeing. No words could describe the feeling," she said.

nary_nodes.label: Total solar eclipse global frequency
evidence: A total solar eclipse happens somewhere on Earth every 18 months or so.

nary_nodes.label: Total solar eclipse local rarity
evidence: But they are much rarer for any given place, only occurring once in roughly 400 years.

nary_nodes.label: Corona definition
evidence: The light coming from the darkness was the Sun's corona - superheated jets of gas thrown thousands of miles out into space.

nary_nodes.label: Prominences definition
evidence: small loops of pink gas called prominences following the Sun's turbulent magnetic field.

nary_nodes.label: Total eclipse is cosmological coincidence
evidence: The fact that we get to experience a total eclipse at all is an incredible cosmological coincidence.

nary_nodes.label: Sun-Earth vs Moon-Earth distance
evidence: The Sun is 150 million kilometres (93 million miles) away from the Earth - 400 times further away than the Moon.

nary_nodes.label: Moon and Sun apparent size explanation
evidence: But because the diameter of the Moon is 400 times less than the Sun's, they appear exactly the same size in our sky.

nary_nodes.label: Hypothetical conditions for no total eclipse
evidence: If the Moon was slightly smaller or its orbit was a little further away from the Earth then we would never see a total eclipse.

nary_nodes.label: Upcoming golden age of total eclipses
evidence: We're about to enter a "golden age" of total solar eclipses between 2026 and 2028.

nary_nodes.label: Future Total Solar Eclipses (2026-2028)
evidence: Eclipse chasers can travel around the world to be wowed by the spectacle of three total solar eclipses in the next couple of years.

nary_nodes.label: Future total eclipses not visible in UK
evidence: But none of these are visible in the UK.

nary_nodes.label: Partial Eclipse in UK (2027)
evidence: The best the country will see is a partial eclipse in 2027 when there will be about 45% coverage in some regions.

nary_nodes.label: UK will not experience fuller eclipse for decades
evidence: It will be decades until the UK experiences a fuller solar eclipse than Wednesday's.

nary_nodes.label: Partial Eclipse in UK (2081)
evidence: That will be in 2081, where up to 99% of the Sun will be covered.

nary_nodes.label: Total Solar Eclipse in UK (2090)
evidence: And the UK's next total solar eclipse will be in 2090.
